subject: ventures/shift-roster-builder
auditor: agent session (Claude), independent audit subagent; see run record
professional: a restaurant or retail operations manager who builds weekly rosters, together with a payroll specialist who checks FLSA weekly and California daily overtime and rest-gap premiums

evidence.correctness: Ran four hand-computed cases through `node cli.mjs --hours|--csv|--rest-under` with fixtures written in the scratchpad. (1) One person at $20/h, Mon-Fri 8am-5pm plus Sat 8am-11am = 48 h. FLSA weekly rule (29 CFR 778.104/.107: 1.5x after 40 h) gives 40*20 + 8*30 = $1,040. The tool printed 'payroll $1,040, 8 overtime hours'. (2) A 13 h Monday shift with `--daily-ot-after 8 --daily-dt-after 12`. California Labor Code 510 gives 8*20 + 4*30 + 1*40 = $320. The tool printed 320.00 with 5.00 overtime hours. (3) Shifts Mon 2pm-10pm and Tue 6am-2pm leave 8 h of rest. At the default `--rest` of 10, a single person leaves Tue UNFILLED, and with `--rest 8` the same person is assigned both, as expected. With two people the tool splits the shifts between them. (4) `--rest-under 11` on the 8 h turnaround at $20 printed '$20' (1 h premium). A plain 8 h shift at $20 with `--burden 10` gives 160 -> 176.00, correct. All 4 matched. Limits: the cases are simple and one-person, I did not verify the multi-person optimiser against an independent ILP (eval/ilp-check.py exists but I did not run it), and only US-style rules are modelled.
evidence.completeness: Full suite `node --test *.test.mjs` (run in background): 264 tests, 264 pass, 0 fail, 438 s. Features I exercised end to end: roster build, open-shift reasons with 'who is at their hour limit' (`--example`), weekly and daily overtime, rest gaps, `--hours`, `--csv`, `--json`, `--rest-under` premium, `--burden`, and `--from-sales` is present in the cli.mjs usage (cli.mjs:67, :114). The README's 'Call-outs from a script' claim (`--cover`) has a test in cli.test.mjs, which passed. Not individually run: server.mjs publish, ICS feeds, webhooks, PWA and the other self-hosting features, which are only covered by server.test.mjs (passing). No TODO or FIXME in calc.mjs, server.mjs or cli.mjs (grep -c gave 0 each). The only 'missing' link hit in index.html was a data: URI favicon, a false positive from my link check.
evidence.verification: Test command `cd ventures/shift-roster-builder && node --test *.test.mjs`: 264/264 pass. Seeded mutation, applied to a COPY of the sources in the scratchpad so the repo tree was never touched (git status on the venture was clean): calc.mjs:497 `Math.max(0, straight - o.otAfter)` changed to `... - o.otAfter - 1`, which shifts the weekly overtime threshold by an hour. `node --test cli.test.mjs` still passed 27/27 (not caught there). `node --test calc.test.mjs` went from 147 passing to 146 passing, 1 failing: 'overtime is priced above the threshold and avoided when someone else can take it'. So the bug was caught, but by exactly one of 264 tests, and the CLI and page tests did not see a wrong overtime hour. That is thin on a core payroll number. The 264 pass count also took 7+ minutes.
evidence.craft: Read calc.mjs (lines 380-520, 2118-2145), demand.mjs header and cli.mjs header. Plain ESM with no dependencies, helpful hard-rule error messages (parseStaff and parseShifts give line-numbered errors), and pure functions. Defects: calc.mjs is a single 2,916-line module that holds parsing, the solver, the dual bounds, payroll, ICS and trades. Overtime is computed in payParts() by bucketing on the day a shift starts, which is documented but means an overnight shift's hours go to the start day (the same convention as the code's comment, fine for FLSA workweek but not for a California midnight split). `seventhDayPay` assumes the workweek starts Monday (calc.mjs:2521 comment). The README is bloated with benchmark tables (about 200 lines) and is hard for a manager to read. The shifts file wants 'Mon, 8am, 5pm' with commas, and the space-separated form 'Mon 8am-5pm' fails with 'could not read the day', which is easy to hit as a first-time user because the error does not hint at the comma format.
evidence.claims: Checked: the page's disclaimer (index.html:79: 'Planning aid, not legal, tax, or financial advice ... does not know your local scheduling-notice, break or minor-labor laws') is present, and cli.mjs repeats it. The 'nothing is uploaded' claim is consistent with index.html:269 and the offline code (not network-audited). The usage-counting opt-out exists (index.html:270). demand.mjs says honestly that it was 'Not tested on a real POS export'. The README optimality claim ('Checked against an exact search: no roster ... scores better by more than $0.50') is printed by the tool, and README honestly reports that the pay-gap was not proven on 0 of 4 hard cases. Not backed or weak: (a) llms.txt links to the old duncan-haywood.github.io Pages address, while CLAUDE.md says the catalogue is now at marisstella.app (the old address only serves redirects), so the product's llms.txt is stale. (b) The README opener says 'After using this, you can now build a week's schedule that nobody has to be moved around in', an outcome claim no file measures. (c) I did not verify README statements that 'Wages, hour caps and payroll never appear on the staff page (tested)' beyond seeing server.test.mjs pass.
evidence.fitness: Job walked through: a manager with a 7-person team writes staff and shifts, runs `node cli.mjs --example` and gets '29 of 32 shifts covered, payroll $3,622, 0 overtime hours', three open shifts each with a reason ('4 people free, but 4 at their weekly hour limit'), and a 'week depends on' ranking. That is the real Sunday-night job and the reasons are actionable. Then wrote my own week (cases above) from scratch and it produced correct rosters and costs. Friction: the comma-separated format is not forgiving (see craft), and the staff tail needs an availability cell like 'Mon-Sun 0-24'. The self-hosting server was not run by me. Paid tools offer time clocks and push notifications, which the README states it does not.
evidence.domain: Compared against FLSA 29 CFR 778 (weekly 1.5x after 40 h, regular rate), California Labor Code 510 (daily 8/12 h tiers, double time), and the Oregon, Seattle and New York City style rest and predictive-scheduling premiums (the tool calls these 'arithmetic on numbers you enter, not a statement of what any law requires'). It matches the 40 h and CA tiers exactly in my cases. Departures: no state-by-state presets (the user must set `--daily-ot-after`, `--rest`, `--premium-hours` themselves), the workweek is fixed Monday to Sunday, no regular-rate adjustment for differentials or bonuses was checked by me (a `diffPerHour` option exists), the 7th-day rule assumes a Monday start, and minor-labor and meal-break rules are explicitly not modelled. A payroll specialist would accept it as a planning aid with those stated limits.

defects.what: Core overtime threshold is protected by a single unit test: shifting the weekly overtime threshold by one hour (mutation at calc.mjs:497) left cli.test.mjs 27/27 green and failed only 1 of 147 calc tests.
First-time input trap: the shifts file needs 'Mon, 8am, 5pm' (commas) and 'Mon 8am-5pm' fails with 'could not read the day', with no hint about the format.
llms.txt links to the retired GitHub Pages address instead of https://marisstella.app/shift-roster-builder/.
calc.mjs is a 2,916-line single module and README carries about 200 lines of benchmark history in the user-facing page, which obscures the manager-facing instructions.
Overtime and rest are bucketed by shift start day and a Monday-start workweek: an overnight shift crossing midnight on a daily-overtime state's boundary is attributed to the start day.

verdict: A real, working weekly rostering tool whose arithmetic I could reproduce: weekly 1.5x overtime ($1,040 on a 48 h week), California daily/double-time tiers ($320 on a 13 h day), rest-gap blocking at 10 h vs 8 h, a one-hour rest premium and burden all matched hand calculation, and all 264 tests pass in 438 s. The seeded overtime-threshold mutation was caught, but by a single test out of 264 and not by the CLI tests, so the safety net on the most payroll-relevant number is thin. The disclaimer and the limits are honest and prominent. It falls short of the bar only on claims (stale llms.txt URL, an unmeasured outcome sentence in the README opener) and craft (monolithic calc.mjs, unfriendly input format error). I did not check the multi-person optimiser against the repo's ILP script, nor run the self-hosted server, so those parts are credited only on their passing tests.
